title: Apply Greg's 60 s abort / 10 s warning rule to Engram's own operation time limits
outcome: Apply Greg's 60 s abort / 10 s warning rule to Engram's own operation time limits
acceptance: Every Engram limit that aborts, kills or resets an operation (for example SQLite busy or lock waits, subprocess and Git exchange deadlines, MCP or control call deadlines, launcher stage limits) is listed with its location and current value, and each is at least 60 s (existing longer limits are kept) or justified on the item as not an operation-aborting limit; an MCP call still in flight when the client itself closes the session either completes whole or writes nothing (nothing partial is written), and is not an Engram abort

An operation still running after 10 s logs one warning naming the operation, without interrupting it; a single blocking system call that runs past 10 s is named when it returns; for a CLI command the caller (the launcher) owns the 10 s warning; Engram's own stderr warning is opt-in and is not written into --json output. A warning never interrupts the operation; a process exit that waits for its caller to drain the caller's own pipe is ordinary pipe behaviour, not an Engram limit. At process end a queued warning is delivered best effort; Engram's own waiting for it is bounded by a short fixed bound (1 s), and a write already handed to the system completes as the system completes it. Every warning writer uses its own output handle, so a warning never holds a lock or wait that the work itself needs. A warning that is late or missing only because the system itself stalls or fails (an output device, or a filesystem operation such as a read or rename that does not complete for more than 10 s) is outside Engram's control and is not guarded against.

Changed limits keep their idempotency and exact-retry semantics: an operation aborted at 60 s leaves no partial durable write, and its retry neither duplicates nor misreports the outcome, shown by tests that observe behaviour
